pre_change_state.caveat_quote: I ran out of tool calls before I could open every relevant paper.

claims.text: It also raised the ethics of handing PARO over and then taking it back [W2778691880].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The abstract lists the ethics of giving and retrieving PARO as one of three issues.

claims.text: | [W1558982838] | Medication-adherence robots at home, crossover RCT (no abstract available; dementia not indicated) |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The record has the title as a randomised cross-over trial on medication adherence at home, and no abstract, so the table row is accurate.

claims.text: **Other settings (snippets):** hospital patient-reported outcome collection [W2946005838], robot-administered cognitive testing in Japan [W2924547041], frailty monitoring [W2939831007].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: All three descriptions match the abstracts: PROM collection, TICS cognitive testing, and frailty monitoring. Japan fits the Japanese TICS version.

claims.text: Social robots may help with agitation, anxiety, quality of life, engagement, loneliness and medication use, but high-quality RCTs are lacking [W2808281222].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The review reports positive impacts on agitation, anxiety and QoL, with improvements in engagement and loneliness and less medication use in the narrative review. It also notes the lack of high-quality studies.

claims.text: **Responses vary a lot between people.** Reflections from an Australian cluster RCT (PARO vs plush toy vs usual care) stress that responses differ between individuals and over time, and raise ethical questions about giving PARO to someone and then taking it away [W2778691880].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The paper is a cluster RCT of PARO versus plush toy and usual care, with variable responses and the ethics of giving and retrieving PARO. Australia fits the author affiliations and the ANZCTR registration.

claims.text: Joy for All pets in UK supported living [W3015009700]
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The study used Joy for All robot animals in supported living facilities. UK is plausible from the authors and is not contradicted.

claims.text: | AIBO and loneliness [W2132164645] | Long-term care residents; dementia not stated |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: AIBO and loneliness in LTCF residents, with no dementia stated, matches the abstract.

claims.text: | **Companion / service robots for the home** | **Hobbit** [W2994761079]; a companion robot in Hungarian homes (Zsiga et al.) [W2717439789]; **MARIO** [W2955051104] | Daily-routine help, reminders, entertainment, fetching objects |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Hobbit, the companion robot in Hungarian homes (the Zsiga et al. authors suggest Hungary) and MARIO are home or companion robots offering routine help, entertainment and similar functions. The MARIO study was in a nursing home, so this is slightly loose but acceptable.

claims.text: | [W3015603533] | Taiwan PARO study: participants had **depression** |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The Taiwan PARO study enrolled older adults with depression.

claims.text: | PARO naturalistic observation [W2039822570]; dog/seal/toy-cat visits [W2294211165] | Dementia status unclear from what I saw |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Naturalistic PARO observation and dog/seal/toy-cat visits are described correctly, and dementia status is unclear in both abstracts.

claims.text: **It listed four papers as "dropped" that were never in the first map:** [W2294211165], [W2521240520], [W1575107006] and [W2094053894].
claims.label: not_a_claim
claims.rationale: This is about the assistant's own process (what it dropped from a map), not a checkable claim about the papers.

claims.text: **NAO vs PARO vs a real dog:** a Spanish nursing home and day centre [W1807810766]
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The abstract covers NAO, PARO and a real dog in a nursing home and day care center. Spanish is plausible from the authors and is not contradicted.

claims.text: Medication-adherence robots, crossover RCT (no abstract available) [W1558982838]
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The record has a randomised cross-over trial on medication adherence and no abstract.

claims.text: | Attitude studies [W2521240520, W1575107006] and the NAO smartpen demo [W2094053894] | No actual robot use with people with dementia |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The two papers are attitude studies and the smartpen/NAO paper is a demo proposal, so none involved actual robot use with people with dementia.

claims.text: **Outcomes are mismatched.** Engagement and affect respond, while standard scales often don't [W2732925385, W2955051104].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The Liang trial found improvements in affect and social interaction but no differences in dementia symptoms, and MARIO showed engagement but no scale changes.

claims.text: **MARIO:** participants stayed engaged and accepted the robot, with no significant change in quality of life, depression or social support (n=10, 4 weeks) [W2955051104].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The abstract reports sustained interest and acceptance, no significant differences in QoL, depression or social support, and n=10 over 4 weeks.

claims.text: In Spain, the PARO group's quality-of-life (QUALID) scores rose, and both robot groups showed less apathy [W1807810766].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: QUALID scores increased in the PARO group, and the robot groups showed improved apathy. Ambiguity over what a higher QUALID score means does not change that the statement reports the record's findings as stated.

claims.text: | Japanese PARO long-term studies [W2148142846, W2043711811] | Abstracts describe "elderly people" in care facilities and give no dementia diagnosis. Check the full texts, since care residents may include people with dementia |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The abstracts describe elderly people in care facilities with no dementia diagnosis stated.

claims.text: | **Health-care / communication robots** | Auckland "HealthBot"/iRobiQ/Cafero programme [W1945345301, W1558982838, W1982844896] | Health monitoring, medication reminders, entertainment |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The papers are about health-care robots, HealthBot and the Auckland programme, with health monitoring and entertainment functions. The iRobiQ/Cafero names are not in the records, but the grouping is not contradicted.

claims.text: **Effects vary by person.** Who benefits depends on dementia severity [W2732925385], individual presentation [W2778691880] and whether the person has pets [W2953482672].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The records support each attribution: cognitive impairment level, individual presentation, and pet ownership affecting interaction with Paro.

claims.text: | **Humanoid** | **NAO** [W1807810766]; **Brian 2.1** [W2046365492]; a Bandit-style exercise coach [W1967507142]; Betty (snippet) [W2944083468] | Group therapy, cognitive games, exercise coaching |
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: The records do not describe a Bandit-style robot for the Fasola paper, and the other humanoid attributions are only loosely supported.

claims.text: | [W2999297198] | Barriers and enablers for humanoid robots in health and social care |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The paper is a systematic review of barriers and enablers for humanoid robots in health and social care.

claims.text: | [W2592259105] | Kubi telepresence, older adults with mobility impairment (snippet) |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The Kubi telepresence usability test involved older adults with mobility impairment.

claims.text: People with less cognitive impairment benefited more [W2732925385].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Subanalyses showed that care recipients with less cognitive impairment responded better to Paro.

claims.text: Barriers and enablers for humanoid robots [W2999297198]
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The review is on barriers and enablers for humanoid robots.

claims.text: They also prompted longer looks and more resident-initiated conversation than visits with a live dog [W1972564462].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The AIBO induced longer looks and more resident-initiated conversation than the live dog.

claims.text: This was an uncontrolled single-group study [W3015603533].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The design was a single-group before-and-after quasi-experiment with no control group.

claims.text: **Ongoing:** a protocol comparing a humanoid robot with tablet training for people with dementia at home [W2975531399].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The protocol compares Pepper with a tablet-based training program for people with dementia at home.

claims.text: **Weak study designs.** Samples are small, studies are short (4–12 weeks) and blinding is poor [W2808281222].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: The review reports high risk of bias in allocation concealment and blinding and calls for larger samples, but it does not state that studies lasted 4–12 weeks.

claims.text: | [W1948807083] | Attitudes towards health-care robots in a retirement village (focus groups and questionnaires) |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The study used focus groups and questionnaires on attitudes toward health-care robots in a retirement village.

claims.text: | Robot companion cats | Own homes | (snippet) [W3034490183] |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The study is on robot cats for people with dementia in their own homes.

claims.text: | **NAO** (humanoid) | Spanish nursing home and day centre | [W1807810766] |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: NAO was used in a nursing home and day care center, and Spanish is plausible from the authors and is not contradicted.

claims.text: **I overstated what the meta-analysis contains.** I said most of the trials in [W2808281222] were dementia trials.
claims.label: not_a_claim
claims.rationale: This is a statement about the assistant's own earlier error, not a checkable claim about the paper's content.

claims.text: | [W2939831007] | Socially assistive robot for frailty monitoring, usability study (snippet) |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The paper is a usability study of a socially assistive robot for monitoring frailty.

claims.text: **Ethics in practice**, such as deception, attachment and withdrawing the robot, is under-studied empirically [W2778691880, W3001702224].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Neither paper states that the ethics of deception and attachment is under-studied empirically.

claims.text: | **PARO** | Day centres, then the person's home (New Zealand) | [W2732925385] |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: PARO was used at day care centers and at home in Auckland, New Zealand.

claims.text: | Japanese multi-robot nursing-home study [W2898061611]; New Zealand health-care robots [W1945345301] | Population not described as having dementia |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The Japanese multi-robot nursing-home study and the New Zealand health-care robots study do not describe the population as having dementia.

claims.text: **Five Japanese nursing homes over 24 weeks:** gains in communication, self-care and social life targets compared with controls, using a quasi-experimental design [W2898061611].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The abstract matches: five Japanese nursing homes, 24 weeks, quasi-experimental, with significant gains in communication, self-care and social life.

claims.text: **Ethics study:** attachment to a robot in a teaching-style setting was low to medium, and showing emotional behaviour did not change acceptance [W3001702224].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Attachment in the didactic setting was low to medium and the robot's emotive behavior did not influence acceptance.

claims.text: | [W2924547041] | Robot-administered cognitive testing with community-dwelling older adults (snippet) |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The study involved robot-administered cognitive testing with community-dwelling older adults.
